title: Why product people should write SQL
summary: What changes when you can answer your own questions, and what this course will and will not cover.
body:
Every product team has a queue of small questions waiting on the data team. Each one takes a minute to answer and a week to get answered. Learning a little SQL closes that gap.

What you will be able to do

  • Count how many people used a feature in a date range
  • Compare behaviour across plans or signup cohorts
  • Spot when a chart in a deck does not add up

By the end of this course you will not be an analyst, and that is fine. You will be someone who can check a hunch before a meeting, and who asks better questions when the hard ones come up.

Try it: Write down three questions you asked someone else for in the last month. We will answer versions of them by the end of the course.

title: A tour of the product database
summary: Meet the four tables used throughout the course: accounts, users, plans and events.
body:
Our practice database belongs to a fictional project tool. It has four tables. Accounts are the paying companies, users belong to accounts, plans describe pricing, and events record what users did and when.

How the tables connect

  • Each user row has an account_id pointing to its account
  • Each account has a plan_id pointing to its plan
  • Each event has a user_id, a name and a timestamp

The events table is the big one. Each row is one action: a project created, a file exported, an invite sent. Almost every product question ends up there.

Try it: Sketch the four tables on paper with arrows between them. Keep the sketch next to you for the rest of the course.

title: Filtering and counting
summary: SELECT, WHERE and COUNT: the three words behind most product questions.
body:
Start with the smallest useful query: count the rows that match a condition. How many exports happened last week? That is a COUNT over events, filtered by name and date.

Patterns to remember

  • COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts people
  • Filter dates with a clear start and end, never just a start
  • Name your columns so the result explains itself

Once counting feels natural, add DISTINCT. Counting events tells you how often something happened. Counting distinct users tells you how many people did it. Most arguments about numbers come from mixing these up.

Try it: Count how many distinct users exported a file in the last 30 days, then how many export events there were. Explain the difference in one sentence.

title: Joins without double counting
summary: Bring accounts, users and plans together, and learn the mistake that inflates every number.
body:
A join lets you ask questions that span tables, like which plan the exporting users are on. The risk is the one-to-many join: join accounts to events and every account appears once per event.

A checklist before every join

  • What does one row of my result represent?
  • Which side has many rows per key?
  • Should I aggregate before joining?

The fix is to decide what one row of your answer should represent before you write the join. If the answer is one row per account, aggregate the events first, then join.

title: Your first activation funnel
summary: Combine everything so far to measure how new teams move from signup to their first shared project.
body:
A funnel is a sequence of steps and a count of how many people reached each one. For our tool: signed up, created a project, invited a teammate, shared a timeline.

Steps in this exercise

  • Define the cohort: accounts created in one month
  • Find the first time each account did each step
  • Count accounts at each step and calculate conversion

Build each step as its own query first. Then combine them, making sure each step only counts people who completed the previous one. Present it as a small table with the percentage that moved on at each step.

Try it: Share your funnel with a teammate and ask them which step they would work on first. Their answer is the start of a good product conversation.

title: The decision behind the dashboard
summary: Why most dashboards fail, and the one question to ask before you draw anything.
body:
A dashboard is a tool for a recurring decision. If you cannot name the decision and who makes it, the dashboard will drift into a wall of charts that nobody reads.

Signs a dashboard has lost its purpose

  • Nobody can say who it is for
  • It has more than twelve charts
  • People screenshot it but never open it

Before choosing any metric, write one sentence: every Monday, the growth team decides where to spend the week, and they need to know which channels are improving.

Try it: Pick a dashboard you own. Write its decision sentence. If you cannot, that is your answer.

title: Choosing the few numbers that matter
summary: Separate the numbers that drive action from the ones that are merely interesting.
body:
For each decision, list the numbers that would change your mind. Those stay. Numbers that are interesting but would not change anything belong in a separate exploration page.

Good headline numbers

  • Change when the thing you care about changes
  • Come with a clear comparison
  • Have a written definition

Aim for three to five headline numbers, each with a comparison: against last period, a target, or a benchmark. A number without a comparison cannot tell you whether to act.

title: Picking the right chart
summary: Lines for trends, bars for comparisons, tables for lookups, and when to skip a chart entirely.
body:
Most dashboards only need four chart types. Line charts show change over time. Bar charts compare categories. Tables are for looking things up. A single big number with a comparison is often the best chart of all.

Quick guide

  • Trend over time: line
  • Compare groups: horizontal bar
  • Exact values: table
  • One status: big number with delta

Avoid pie charts with more than three slices, dual axes, and anything three dimensional. They make readers work hard to get a worse answer.

Try it: Redraw one chart from your current dashboard using this guide and compare which one your team understands faster.

title: Layout, colour and attention
summary: Arrange a dashboard so the most important thing is seen first.
body:
People read dashboards like pages: top left first, then across and down. Put the headline numbers at the top, the trends that explain them underneath, and the detail at the bottom.

Layout rules

  • Headline numbers in the first row
  • Explanations in the second
  • Detail and tables last

Use one accent colour for the thing that needs attention, and grey for everything else. When everything is colourful, nothing stands out.

title: Keeping dashboards trusted
summary: Definitions, owners and a yearly clean-up keep numbers believable.
body:
Trust breaks the first time two dashboards disagree. Give every metric a written definition and an owner, and link to the definition from the chart itself.

A simple governance routine

  • Every metric has a definition and an owner
  • Dashboards show when data was last refreshed
  • Unused dashboards are archived quarterly

Once a quarter, look at usage. Archive anything that has not been opened in ninety days. A smaller set of trusted dashboards beats a large set of doubtful ones.

title: What a design system is for
summary: Design systems exist to make good decisions repeatable. Here is how to tell if your team needs one.
body:
A design system is a set of shared decisions: colours, type, spacing, components and the rules for using them. Its job is to let a team ship consistent interfaces without re-deciding the basics every time.

Signals you need a system

  • The same button exists in six slightly different styles
  • New screens take longer than they should
  • Engineers ask designers the same questions repeatedly

Not every team needs a full system. If you have one product and three designers, a well-kept component library and a page of guidelines may be enough.

Try it: List three decisions your team re-makes on every project. They are your first candidates for the system.

title: Running an interface audit
summary: Screenshot everything, group it, and count the inconsistencies. It is the fastest way to win support.
body:
Take screenshots of every screen in your product and paste them onto one big board. Then group similar elements together: all the buttons, all the form fields, all the headings.

What to collect

  • Buttons and links
  • Form fields and validation messages
  • Colours, type sizes and spacing values

Count what you find. Saying we have 14 shades of grey and 9 button styles is far more persuasive than saying things feel inconsistent.

Try it: Do a one-hour audit of just your buttons. Share the board in your team channel and see what reaction you get.

title: Design tokens: colour, type, space
summary: Turn the audit into a small set of named values that everyone shares.
body:
Tokens are named values such as color-text-primary or space-4. They let design tools and code share the same decisions, and they make big changes like a rebrand much cheaper.

Naming tips

  • Name by purpose, not appearance: text-muted, not grey-500
  • Keep scales short and predictable
  • Document which tokens are safe to use directly

Start small: a neutral scale, one brand colour, a status palette, a type scale of six sizes and a spacing scale based on a single unit.

title: Building your first components
summary: Buttons, inputs and cards: variants, states and the props that matter.
body:
Pick the three components used most in your audit. For each one, list its variants (primary, secondary), sizes and states (hover, focus, disabled, loading).

Every component needs

  • Clear variants with a reason for each
  • Visible focus states
  • Guidance on when not to use it

Design every state before you build anything. Focus and error states are where most inconsistencies hide, and they matter most for accessibility.

title: Documentation and adoption
summary: Write docs people read, and make the system the easiest path for your team.
body:
Good documentation answers the questions people actually ask: which component do I use here, and how do I use it correctly? Lead with examples and do's and don'ts rather than long explanations.

Documentation that works

  • An example first, explanation second
  • Do and don't pairs
  • A changelog for every release

Adoption is a product problem. Pair with teams on their next feature, collect feedback, and release small improvements often with clear notes on what changed.

Try it: Write the documentation page for your button component in under 300 words.

title: How type works on screens
summary: x-height, contrast and spacing: what makes a typeface readable at 14 pixels.
body:
Interface text is small and read quickly, so the typeface needs a generous x-height, open shapes and even spacing. Many beautiful display faces fall apart below 18 pixels.

What to look for

  • Large x-height relative to cap height
  • Clear difference between l, I and 1
  • Several weights, including a true medium

Test candidates with real interface copy, at real sizes, on real screens, including a cheap laptop and a phone in sunlight.

Try it: Set the same paragraph in three typefaces at 15 pixels and ask a colleague which is easiest to read.

title: Pairing typefaces
summary: One family is often enough. When you pair, pair for contrast.
body:
Many great interfaces use a single family in two or three weights. If you pair, choose fonts that are clearly different, such as a serif for headings and a sans for text, but share proportions.

Safe pairing patterns

  • Serif headings with sans body
  • Grotesque headings with humanist body
  • One family with a monospace for data

Avoid pairing two similar sans-serifs. The result looks like a mistake rather than a choice.

title: Building a type scale
summary: Pick a ratio, generate sizes, and name them by role.
body:
A type scale is a short list of sizes generated from a base size and a ratio. A base of 16 pixels and a ratio of 1.25 gives 16, 20, 25, 31 and 39.

Steps

  • Choose a base size for body text
  • Choose a ratio between 1.2 and 1.333
  • Round the results and name them by role

Name each step by its role, such as body, lead, title and display, so designers and engineers talk about the same thing.

Try it: Build a six-step scale for your product and replace any sizes in your current design that are not on it.

title: Line length, leading and rhythm
summary: The small settings that make long text comfortable.
body:
Aim for 50 to 75 characters per line for body text. Longer lines tire the eye. Shorter lines break the reading rhythm.

Comfortable defaults

  • Body: 16 to 18 pixels, line height 1.5 to 1.7
  • Headings: line height 1.1 to 1.25
  • Max width around 65 characters

Line height around 1.5 suits body text, while large headings look better tighter, around 1.1 to 1.2. Space between paragraphs should be clearly larger than the space between lines.

title: Hierarchy without shouting
summary: Use size, weight and colour together so pages scan easily.
body:
Hierarchy tells readers what to look at first. You have three main tools: size, weight and colour. Using all three at maximum on every heading creates noise.

Check your hierarchy

  • Squint at the page: does the right thing stand out?
  • Is there one clear primary heading?
  • Is secondary text visibly quieter?

Try reducing contrast instead of adding it. A muted colour for secondary text often does more than a bigger heading.

title: Discovery as a weekly habit
summary: Why small, continuous discovery beats big research projects.
body:
Teams that talk to a customer every week make better decisions than teams that run one big study a year. Small, regular conversations keep assumptions fresh and make it normal to change your mind.

A sustainable rhythm

  • One customer conversation a week
  • A shared place for notes
  • A short review with the team every two weeks

The goal of this course is to make discovery a routine part of the week rather than a phase before building.

Try it: Book one customer conversation for next week before you start the next lesson.

title: Interviews that reveal behaviour
summary: Ask about specific past events, not opinions or wishes.
body:
People are poor at predicting what they will do, but good at describing what they did. Ask about the last time something happened: tell me about the last time you prepared a client report.

Good interview questions

  • Tell me about the last time you...
  • What happened next?
  • What did you try before that?

Follow the story. Ask what happened next, what was hard and what they tried. Avoid pitching your idea during the interview.

title: Mapping opportunities
summary: Turn interview notes into a map of needs, pain points and desires.
body:
After a few interviews, group what you heard into opportunities: needs, pain points and desires. Arrange them under the outcome your team is trying to improve.

Building the map

  • Start with one clear outcome
  • Add opportunities heard in interviews
  • Group related opportunities and pick one to explore

The map helps you compare options. Instead of debating features, you debate which opportunity matters most for the outcome.

Try it: Map the opportunities from your last three customer conversations on one page.

title: Finding the riskiest assumption
summary: Every idea rests on assumptions. Test the one that would sink it.
body:
For any idea, list what must be true for it to work: people want it, they can use it, it is feasible, and it is viable for the business.

Kinds of assumption

  • Desirability: do people want this?
  • Usability: can they figure it out?
  • Feasibility and viability: can we build and sustain it?

Rank the assumptions by how important they are and how little evidence you have. Test the one in the top corner first.

title: Small, fast experiments
summary: Prototypes, fake doors and one-day tests that answer one question each.
body:
Good experiments are small and answer one question. A clickable prototype can test usability. A short survey after a real task can test desirability. A spreadsheet model can test viability.

Before you run a test

  • Which assumption does it test?
  • What result would change our mind?
  • How quickly can we run it?

Decide in advance what result would change your plan. Without that, every result looks like support for what you already wanted to do.

title: What a spec is really for
summary: Specs exist to align people on a problem and a decision, not to describe every pixel.
body:
A spec is a shared understanding written down. It helps the team agree on the problem, the outcome and the boundaries before work starts.

A spec should answer

  • What problem are we solving and for whom?
  • How will we know it worked?
  • What are we deliberately not doing?

Long specs are rarely read. Aim for one page that links out to details, designs and research.

title: A structure that works
summary: Problem, outcome, proposal, scope, open questions.
body:
Use the same five headings for every spec so readers know where to look: problem, outcome, proposal, scope and non-goals, and open questions.

The five sections

  • Problem, with evidence
  • Outcome and how it will be measured
  • Proposal, scope and non-goals, open questions

Write the problem section first and share it before writing the rest. Agreement on the problem saves more time than anything else.

Try it: Rewrite your last spec into these five headings and see what was missing.

title: Problems before solutions
summary: Describe the problem with evidence so the team can propose better solutions.
body:
If the spec starts with the solution, the team debates the solution. If it starts with a well-evidenced problem, engineers and designers often propose something better.

Evidence to include

  • Customer quotes
  • Usage numbers
  • Support tickets or sales notes

Use quotes from customers, numbers from analytics and examples from support tickets. Specific evidence beats general claims.

title: Scope and non-goals
summary: Saying what you will not do is the most useful sentence in a spec.
body:
Non-goals stop scope creep before it starts. They also show stakeholders that you considered their idea and chose to leave it out for now.

Writing non-goals

  • Name the tempting extension you are leaving out
  • Say why, briefly
  • Say when you might revisit it

Keep scope as a short list of capabilities rather than a list of screens. It leaves room for design to find the best solution.

Try it: Add three non-goals to a spec you are working on.

title: Keeping specs alive
summary: Update the spec when decisions change, and keep a short decision log.
body:
Plans change once work starts. Update the spec when they do, and add a dated line to a decision log at the bottom so people can see what changed and why.

Habits that help

  • A decision log at the bottom
  • A clear status at the top
  • A short outcome note after launch

When the work ships, add a short note on the outcome. Over time your specs become a record of what the team learned.

title: Your first ninety days
summary: What changes when you become a manager, and how to spend your first three months.
body:
Your job is no longer to do the work yourself but to help a team do its best work. That shift feels uncomfortable, and that is normal.

A simple ninety-day plan

  • Month one: meet everyone and listen
  • Month two: fix one or two small frustrations
  • Month three: agree on goals together

Spend the first month listening, the second month making small improvements, and the third month setting direction together with your team.

Try it: Write down what you think your team needs most. Revisit the note after your first round of one-to-ones.

title: One-to-ones that matter
summary: The meeting that builds trust: their agenda, every week, protected.
body:
A one-to-one belongs to the person you manage. Let them set the agenda and keep the time protected, even in busy weeks.

Good one-to-one habits

  • Weekly or every two weeks, at a regular time
  • Their agenda first, yours second
  • Shared notes with clear follow-ups

Use a few open questions to get started when they have nothing planned: what is on your mind, what is getting in your way, what could I do differently?

title: Feedback that is specific and kind
summary: A simple structure for positive and critical feedback.
body:
Feedback works best when it is specific, timely and about behaviour rather than personality. Describe the situation, the behaviour and the impact, then ask for their view.

Situation, behaviour, impact

  • In yesterday's planning meeting
  • you summarised the trade-offs clearly
  • and the team made a decision in ten minutes

Give positive feedback often and in detail. It tells people what to keep doing and makes critical feedback easier to hear.

Try it: Give one piece of specific positive feedback today using this structure.

title: Delegating outcomes
summary: Hand over problems and results, not lists of tasks.
body:
Delegating tasks keeps you as the bottleneck. Delegating outcomes, such as reducing onboarding drop-off by a fifth, gives people room to think and grow.

When you delegate

  • Describe the outcome and why it matters
  • Agree on check-ins
  • Be clear about decision rights

Agree on what done looks like, when you will check in and what decisions they can make without you.

title: Meetings people do not dread
summary: Fewer, shorter meetings with a clear purpose and a written outcome.
body:
Every recurring meeting should have a purpose, an owner and a written outcome. If it has none of these, try cancelling it for a month.

Meeting checklist

  • Is the purpose written in the invite?
  • Do we leave with decisions and owners?
  • Could this be a written update?

Keep status updates in writing and use meeting time for discussion and decisions.

Try it: Audit your team's recurring meetings and cancel or shorten one this week.
